name: Equites Promoti Illyriciani (limitan)

abilities.name: Rapid Advance
abilities.text: Improved unit movement speed over an extended period.

attributes.name: Hide (forest)
attributes.text: This unit can hide in forests until enemy units get too close.

short: The name Illyriciani probably derives from the name of the Praetorian prefecture of Illyricum (Latin-praefectura praetorio per Illyricum). In the 2nd-4th centuries Illyricum and other Danubian provinces (Raetia, Pannonia, Moesia) had the largest concentration of Roman troops (up to a third of the entire army) and were the main recruiting area. A large number (23 entries) of units with this name, recorded in the Notitia Dignitatum, belong exclusively to the limitanei. Promoti in Latin means «promoted, raised» and appears to have been originally applied to individual soldiers, but in time already groups of such chosen legionaries began to be trained in the skill of horsemanship. This led, especially in the 3rd century, to the forming of legionary cavalry units, which then appear to have been increasingly detached for use as independent units. This, in turn, led to the large number of Equites promoti units found in the Notitia Dignitatum - though mostly as part of limitanei rather than field armies. Equites - a new type of cavalry appeared in the 3rd century (probably under Diocletian), has nothing in common with the ancient Roman class of Equites (cavalrymen) or legionary cavalry of the Principate period (equites legionis). Literally translated from Latin as «horsemen», it is a cavalry unit of any type.
history: Since Rome's beginnings, as was common in almost all ancient societies, the noble class were the only people who could afford horses, and were therefore most likely to own one. As a result, early Roman armies fielded cavalry consisting entirely of nobles - the equestrian class - and then bolstered their comparatively small numbers with units formed from the city's Italian Socii allies. Due to a number of high profile defeats, such as their poor showing during Hannibal's climactic Italian campaign at the end of the 3rd century BC, Roman cavalry contingents were generally considered to be far weaker than their Italian counterparts whilst purely a unit of nobles. Eventually the Socii were granted Roman citizenship and, following a number of reforms to the army's structure, were folded into its ranks. Wherever the Romans went after that they drew on local specialists to swell their numbers as auxiliary troops. By the time of the Hunnic incursions, auxiliaries had been made a part of the Legions, resulting in Rome being able to field some of the best, most adaptable cavalry in the ancient world.
strengths: Very low damage and armour penetration
